reasons: The route guards and routes, which carry the access rules, were not visible.

terms.meaning: A rule that connects a web address to a page.
Loading a page's code only when the user first opens it.
A wrapper that shows a fallback screen instead of crashing the whole app when one page fails.
Shared storage that remembers data fetched from the server so screens do not refetch it each time.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and page list
sections.what: Brings in the routing library, the page-loading helper, the error boundary, the data cache and the UI widgets. It also declares each page the app can show, such as the landing, home, explore, analysis, company and portfolio pages, each loaded only when first needed.
sections.why: Likely reason: loading pages on demand keeps the first screen fast.
sections.watch_out: A page declared here is expected to also have a route further down the file, or it will never appear.

sections.name: DatumRedirect
sections.title: Old Datum address redirect
sections.what: When someone opens the old Datum address, this sends them to the Reality Scan tool instead. If the address had an industries filter, the filter is carried over to the new address.
sections.why: The code comment says Datum is retired and Reality Scan is the current tool. That comment is the only stated reason.
sections.watch_out: If the industries filter is later renamed on the Reality Scan page, old links will silently lose their filter.

sections.name: ProtectedRoute
sections.title: Sign-in required page guard
sections.what: Lets a page show only to signed-in people. A visitor who is not signed in is sent to the login page, and the address they wanted is passed along so they return there after logging in.
sections.why: Likely reason: keep pages private while letting people come back to the page they asked for.
sections.watch_out: The return address is placed inside the web address, so any change to this redirect must keep it properly encoded.

sections.name: AdminRoute
sections.title: Admin-only page guard
sections.what: Works like the sign-in guard but also requires the admin role. Signed-in users who are not admins are sent to the nuclear industry home page instead of seeing the page.
sections.why: Likely reason: restrict admin tools such as company, source and data quality pages to administrators.
sections.watch_out: This check runs in the browser only. The real protection has to be enforced by the server, which is not shown here.

sections.name: IndustryHomeRouter
sections.title: Industry address routing
sections.what: Decides what an address like the industry page for a given name shows. Unknown industries show the general industry page. Known industries go to a guard that shows the main dashboard if the industry is live, and otherwise the general page.
sections.why: The code comment says live industries get the dashboard and other industries get the general page.
sections.watch_out: This depends on the industry lookup returning nothing for unknown names; a change to that lookup would change what this page shows.

sections.name: LiveOnly
sections.title: Live-only workspace guard
sections.what: Guards the workspace pages for each industry. Unknown industries go to the home page and signed-out visitors go to login. For industries not marked live, the app first checks whether any project data exists, showing a loading message or an error with a retry button while it does. If data exists the page opens, otherwise the fallback page is shown.
sections.why: The code comment says only live industries have a working workspace, and the nuclear industry uses older paths.
sections.watch_out: The order of these checks matters. Moving the data check or the sign-in check could expose a page to people or industries it should not reach.

sections.name: useShowTopNav
sections.title: Top navigation bar visibility
sections.what: Decides whether the top navigation bar can show, which is only when the page is inside an industry context.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: If the industry context is missing on a page, the top navigation bar disappears without any message.

sections.name: Router (part 1)
sections.title: Main address list, first half
sections.what: The first part of the list that maps web addresses to pages. It covers the launcher, the Yard, the portfolio views, the login page and the live tool pages, and it redirects the old opportunity map and guided demo addresses. The login page sends people to the tools page while sign-in is switched off.
sections.why: Likely reason: one list decides where each address goes, and a switch disables login during development. The code comment states the switch behaviour.
sections.watch_out: Order matters because the first matching route wins, so a new route placed after a broad one may never be reached.

sections.name: Router (part 2)
sections.title: Main address list, second half
sections.what: The rest of the address list for the industry workspace, covering summary, forecast, dataset, directory, map, explore, analysis, pipeline, glossary, plants, companies, sources and data quality pages, plus a single plant page. Unmatched addresses show the not-found page.
sections.why: Likely reason: each industry has its own set of address paths, so the same pages can be reused for every industry.
sections.watch_out: The directory view shows the companies page, so changing one of these affects the other.

sections.name: App
sections.title: Application shell
sections.what: The outermost part of the app. It sets up the shared data cache, the tooltip system, the address system using the build's base path, notification messages, an error boundary that offers a home link if a page crashes, and a loading message while pages load. It then shows the routing list.
sections.why: Likely reason: standard setup that wraps every page so shared services and error handling are always present.
sections.watch_out: The base path comes from the build setting. A wrong setting would break every link in the app.

summary: The root file of the capital projects web app. It loads the pages on demand and sets up the routing and shared helpers.
purpose: Decides which page to show for each web address and wraps the app with shared services.
why: Likely reason: loading pages only when first needed makes the first screen load faster. Reason for the routing layout not stated in the visible lines.
how: 1. Imports the router, the lazy-loading helper, the error boundary, the query cache and UI widgets. 2. Declares each page as a lazily loaded component. 3. Imports the industry list, sign-in state and industry context. 4. The remaining sections (not supplied) define route guards and the routes.
inputs: The browser address, the sign-in state and the industry list.
outputs: The chosen page, drawn inside shared layout and error handling.
risks: AUTH_DISABLED is imported here; if that switch is on in a live build, sign-in checks are bypassed. Only the imports were supplied, so the routing and guards were not reviewed.
debug: If a page is blank, check its lazy import name here and its route further down the file. If a page needs sign-in but opens anyway, check the AUTH_DISABLED value.
